name: Sufism
line: Seek the divine through love, music and remembrance.

quote.text: Listen to the reed how it tells a tale, complaining of separations.
quote.source: Masnavi, Book 1, line 1, trans. R. A. Nicholson

quotes.text: Truly, in the remembrance of God hearts find rest.
My heart has become capable of every form. I follow the religion of Love: whatever way Love’s camels take, that is my religion and my faith.
quotes.source: Tarjumān al-Ashwāq, trans. R. A. Nicholson

quotes.text: The children of Adam are limbs of one body, created from one essence.
O God, if I worship You for fear of Hell, burn me in Hell; if I worship You in hope of Paradise, exclude me from it; but if I worship You for Your own sake, do not withhold Your everlasting beauty.
quotes.source: Attributed to Rābiʿa in later Sufi tradition

quotes.text: Let us love and be loved. The world belongs to no one.

words.meaning: Sufism; the inner path of Islam
words.usage: What Sufis call their own way.
Repeating divine names or phrases, aloud or in the heart.
Music and poetry heard as a way of remembering. Turkish: sema.
The love that burns away everything but the Beloved.
The steadier word for the love between God and the servant.
The ego’s claim dissolves in awareness of God.
What follows fanāʾ: returning to the world, living through God.
The declaration that God is one. Sufis seek to taste it, not only to affirm it.
The organ of spiritual perception, to be polished like a mirror.
It has stages: commanding, self-blaming, at peace.
The breath of God in the human being.
Mevlevi, Qādirī, Chishtī, Naqshbandī and many more.

words.meaning: The revealed law; the broad road
words.usage: For classical Sufis the path stands on it, as a circle’s radius stands on its rim.
What the path leads to.
Knowing by tasting, as opposed to knowing about.
Also shaykh, or pīr in Persian. The path is travelled with one.
The seeker who has given allegiance to a guide.
Arabic: faqīr. One who knows their need of God.
A blessing that flows through holy people and places.
A saying: all of Sufism is adab.
The first station of the path.
Tie your camel, then trust.
Steadiness under hardship without complaint.
Thanks in ease, and, harder, in difficulty.
From a saying of the Prophet: to worship God as though you see Him.
Given, not earned. Contrasted with maqām, a station that is attained.
Turkish: sohbet. Much of the teaching happens here.
Novices in the Mevlevi lodges began with a thousand and one days in the kitchen.
Cut from the reed bed and crying to return: the opening image of the Masnavi.
The simplest name, breathed in dhikr.
Turkish: tekke. Arabic: zāwiya.

words.meaning: A friend of God; a saint
words.usage: Plural awliyāʾ. Their tombs are visited across the Muslim world.

practices.name: Dhikr
practices.instructions: Sit quietly, upright, with your attention at the heart. Let the breath settle. Then repeat one short phrase of remembrance in time with the breath, silently or just audibly, for fifteen minutes, returning to it whenever the mind wanders. If you are Muslim, use the formulas of your tradition, such as Lā ilāha illā Allāh. If you are not, use a word of your own that points beyond yourself: peace, thank you, light.
practices.why: The Qur’an says that hearts find rest in the remembrance of God. For Sufis, dhikr polishes the heart as one polishes a mirror, until it reflects what is there.
variations: Count ninety-nine repetitions on beads.
Carry the phrase silently through one routine task.
Attend a public dhikr as a guest, if a local community welcomes visitors.

practices.name: A line of love
practices.instructions: Write one line of love to whoever or whatever you love most today: a person, a place, God, the morning. Do not make it clever. Rumi’s followers wrote to the Beloved, and the Beloved is whoever you give your heart to. Read it aloud once, and carry it with you as you go out.
practices.why: ʿIshq, passionate love, is the engine of Sufi poetry. Hafez, Rumi and Yunus Emre all write about love as the way to the divine. One line is a good place to begin.
variations: Write it on a card and leave it for someone.
Write it in your own language and then in another.
Say it aloud to the sky.

practices.name: Open with a phrase
practices.instructions: Before you speak to anyone, say a short phrase of thanks or remembrance. If you are Muslim, it may be Bismillah, in the name of God. If not, choose peace, thank you, or one line of a poem you love. Say it slowly and mean it. The first words of the day set the tone, and they can be the best you know.
practices.why: The first rule of this Onda is to begin with remembrance and end with gratitude. A phrase on waking is the easiest way to keep it.
variations: Say it before you touch your phone.
Say it with a hand on your heart.
Learn one phrase in a language you do not speak.

practices.name: Three dates and water
practices.instructions: Eat three dates, slowly, with a glass of water. Taste the sweetness and think of all the travellers, in all the deserts, who have eaten this food. If you cannot find dates, use any simple sweet fruit. Eating plainly and with thanks is an old Sufi habit, and a pleasant one.
practices.why: Dates and water are the classic way to break a fast in the Muslim world. They carry a long history of travel, hospitality and gratitude.
variations: Share them with someone.
Eat them outside, in the morning light.
Say thank you aloud after the last one.

practices.name: Breathe like a reed
practices.instructions: Sit and breathe slowly in through the nose, and out through softly shaped lips as if playing a flute. Imagine you are a reed, hollow, and that each out-breath is a note. Do ten breaths. Listen for the empty place inside you that the breath moves through. Rumi’s Masnavi begins with a reed that cries because it was cut from its reed bed.
practices.why: The ney, the reed flute, is the instrument of the Mevlevi order and the symbol of the soul longing for its source. Breathing like a reed is a gentle way to feel that longing.
variations: Listen to a ney recording first.
Do it by an open window.
Hum one low note on the out-breath.

practices.name: Adab in the first hour
practices.instructions: For the first hour after you are up, treat every person and every task with adab, courtesy. Greet people warmly, say please and thank you, tidy as you go, and speak softly. Do not rush. Adab is not stiffness. It is attention to the other, made visible in small manners.
practices.why: Adab, right conduct, is at the centre of Sufi training. Teachers say the first thing a student learns is manners, because they are the shape that love takes in everyday life.
variations: Do it for the whole morning.
Say good morning properly to everyone.
Hold a door for each person.

practices.name: Read a poem aloud
practices.instructions: Take one short poem or passage by Rumi, Hafez, ʿAṭṭār, Yunus Emre or Rābiʿa, in a translation made from the original language. Read it aloud, slowly, twice. Notice which line catches. Say that line once more and carry it with you.
practices.why: Sufi teaching travelled as verse, recited and sung, long before it was read silently. The poems were made for the ear and the breath.
variations: Read it to another person.
Copy the line that caught you by hand.
Compare a scholarly translation with a popular version and see what changed.

practices.name: Hospitality
practices.instructions: Offer something to drink or eat to someone, a guest, a neighbour, a colleague. Serve them before yourself. Pay attention to the small things: the cup, the pouring, the moment you hand it over. Ask for nothing. If no one is near, make tea for an empty chair and leave it for the next person who comes.
practices.why: Generosity toward guests is a central part of Sufi manners (adab). Many stories treat a guest as a carrier of something larger than themselves.
variations: Do it quietly, without telling anyone why.
Bring something to a neighbour.
Give your seat or your time.

practices.name: See your own fault first
practices.instructions: Think of someone who has irritated you today. Before you judge them, ask: where is this in me? Write one fault of your own that matches it, and one thing you will do to mend it. Let the other person off the hook, at least in your heart. Sufi teachers say, look at your own fault before another’s.
practices.why: The rule of this Onda is to see the fault in yourself first. Rumi tells many stories in which the one who points at others is shown their own face.
variations: Do it before sending a hard message.
Do it for a public figure you dislike.
Do it kindly: a smile, not a scold.

practices.name: An hour without gossip
practices.instructions: For one hour, say nothing about anyone who is not present, unless it is good. When the urge comes, notice it and let it pass, or turn it into a compliment. See how often talk slides toward gossip, and how much lighter you feel without it. No gossip is a Sufi rule, and a respite.
practices.why: Backbiting is among the things a Sufi guide asks students to leave behind. Silence about others is a protection for both sides, and it is surprisingly restful.
variations: Keep it for a whole day.
Turn each urge into a thank you.
Tell a friend you are trying it.

practices.name: One hidden service
practices.instructions: Do one small service in a shared space and tell nobody: wash the cups, wipe the table, sweep the step, refill the paper. Khidma, service, is the oldest Sufi training. Do it with the same care you would give a guest, and let it go unnoticed.
practices.why: In Sufi lodges the newcomer began in the kitchen and at the door, doing humble work. Service cuts the ego down to size and makes the heart soft.
variations: Do it at work.
Do it in your own home, for someone else.
Do it in a public place, like picking up litter.

practices.name: Find your own Simorgh
practices.instructions: Sit somewhere quiet outdoors and watch the birds for fifteen minutes. In ʿAṭṭār’s Conference of the Birds, thirty birds cross seven valleys to find their king, the Simorgh, and discover that si morgh means thirty birds. They find themselves. Watch, and ask what you have been looking for outside that may be near.
practices.why: ʿAṭṭār’s twelfth-century poem is one of the great Sufi allegories. The birds’ journey stands for the soul’s, and the ending is a mirror.
variations: Read a page of the poem first.
Watch a single bird for five minutes.
Draw one bird and write what it seems to say.

practices.name: Listen to sama
practices.instructions: Put on one piece of Sufi music: a Mevlevi ceremony, qawwali from South Asia, a solo ney. Sit, close your eyes and do nothing else for twenty minutes. Let the music do its work. If you feel moved to sway, let it happen. When it ends, stay in the silence for a minute.
practices.why: Samāʿ means listening. The orders that use music hold that a prepared heart hears in it the call home. Rumi’s followers turned it into the whirling ceremony.
variations: Listen to the same piece every evening for a week.
Follow a translation of the words as you listen.
Watch a recording of the Mevlevi sema from Konya.

practices.name: Night stillness
practices.instructions: When the house is quiet and the lights are low, sit or stand in stillness for fifteen minutes. Look back over the day: where you were heedless, where you were grateful, whom you served, whom you wronged. Ask forgiveness where it is needed, give thanks, and then simply be present until the time is up.
practices.why: The last third of the night is the Sufis’ chosen hour. Rābiʿa is said to have prayed on her roof: the stars are shining, kings have shut their doors, every lover is alone with the beloved.
variations: Step outside and look at the sky.
Keep the first hour after waking silent instead.
End with one line of poetry learned by heart.

practices.name: Hum a melody
practices.instructions: Hum a slow tune with no words, one that you love, for ten minutes, as you cook, tidy or sit. Let it be a wordless prayer. Hum low, so you feel it in the chest. Notice that humming sets the breath in order and the mind quiet. If a verse arrives, let it come.
practices.why: Sufi traditions use voice and melody to settle the heart. Even without words, humming does what samāʿ does: it makes the listener of the singer.
variations: Hum along to a recording.
Hum a lullaby for someone.
Hum while walking.

practices.name: Close with gratitude
practices.instructions: List five things you are grateful for today, in full sentences, and why. Include one thing you would not usually count: a stranger’s smile, a warm bed, a closed door. End with a short thank you to whoever or whatever you feel is behind it all. This is shukr, gratitude, the closing of the day in the Sufi manner.
practices.why: The first rule of this Onda is to begin with remembrance and end with gratitude. Shukr is the habit of noticing what has been given, and it is said to be the key to more.
variations: Say them aloud to someone.
Write them on slips and keep them in a jar.
Write five for someone else, and give them.

practices.name: Stir a halva
practices.instructions: Make semolina halva: toast semolina in butter, add warm sweetened milk or water, and stir until it comes together. Stir slowly and attentively, and think of someone you want to share it with. Then share it. In Turkey, halva is made and given in memory of the dead, and in celebration of the living.
practices.why: Irmik helvası is cooked slowly, and stirring is a kind of meditation. Giving it away is the final step, and turns a dessert into a gift.
variations: Stir it for a neighbour.
Make it in memory of someone.
Cook it with a child.

practices.name: Tell a Rumi story
practices.instructions: Read or recall one short story from Rumi’s Masnavi, and tell it to someone in your own words: the lion and the hare, the Chinese and the Greek painters, the man who lost his ring in the dark and looked for it in the light. End by asking what they think it is about. Stories are how a teaching is passed.
practices.why: The Masnavi is a long poem of tales within tales. Rumi told them aloud, and they are made to be told again. The stories work on you like a good friend’s advice.
variations: Tell it to a child.
Tell it in two minutes.
Look up three versions and compare.

practices.name: A night of tea and poems
practices.instructions: Invite two or three friends for a quiet evening: tea, something sweet, a candle, and a few poems read aloud in turns. Each person brings one poem that moved them. Read, listen, say nothing clever. At the end, sit for a minute in silence. People have met this way for centuries.
practices.why: Poetry gatherings with tea and quiet music are a long tradition across the Persian and Turkish worlds. They are an evening of company, listening and love of words.
variations: Hold it online with distant friends.
Have each person read in a language of their own.
Make it a monthly custom.

practices.name: In the last third of the night
practices.instructions: Once in a while, if you sleep well and it suits you, wake in the last hours of the night and sit for twenty minutes in the dark, quietly, with a glass of water. The Sufis prized this hour as the time when the world is still. Then go back to sleep. If you cannot sleep again, read a poem and rest.
practices.why: The last third of the night is called the hour of closeness in Sufi tradition. Even a short wake in the quiet changes how the next day feels.
variations: Do it with the window open.
Do it with a candle.
Do it once a month on a night you can lie in the next day.

immersePlan.name: Read the opening of the Masnavi
immersePlan.text: Read the opening of Book One, the song of the reed, and one of the stories that follow. Read aloud, slowly. Notice what the reed misses.

immersePlan.name: Read a page of the Conference of the Birds
immersePlan.text: Open ʿAṭṭār’s poem about the birds that cross seven valleys to find their king. Read a few pages, and look for the moment the birds start to complain.

immersePlan.name: Read a song by Yunus Emre
immersePlan.text: Read a few of Yunus Emre’s plain Turkish songs. They are short and warm. Pick one that says what you need today, and read it twice.

immersePlan.name: Watch Sufi Soul
immersePlan.text: Watch William Dalrymple’s documentary on Sufi music from Syria and Turkey to Pakistan and Morocco. Notice how each place sings the same longing in its own voice.

immersePlan.name: Watch Bab’Aziz
immersePlan.text: Watch Nacer Khemir’s film of a blind dervish and his granddaughter crossing the desert to a gathering. It is slow and lovely. Notice how stories are told within it.

immersePlan.name: Watch a Mevlevi sema as a guest
immersePlan.text: Watch a complete recording of the Mevlevi sema from Konya, not a clip. Four salutations, each with its own music. Watch with respect, as a guest, and do not try to imitate it.

immersePlan.name: Listen to Nusrat’s Shahen-Shah
immersePlan.text: Play Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan’s qawwali, devotional song of the Chishti shrines by its greatest modern voice. Let it build; qawwali takes time to rise.

immersePlan.name: Listen to Mevlevi music
immersePlan.text: Play the ney-led music of the whirling ceremony, in a recording by the Kudsi Erguner Ensemble. Close your eyes and follow the reed.

immersePlan.name: Listen to a solo ney
immersePlan.text: Play a taksim, a solo ney improvisation. One breath, one reed, the sound of the first line of the Masnavi. Listen to the whole piece without doing anything else.

immersePlan.name: Look at Rumi’s tomb
immersePlan.text: Look at pictures of the tomb at Konya under its fluted turquoise dome. Visitors of every faith have come for centuries. Notice the dome, and the colour, and where your eye comes to rest.

immersePlan.name: Look at The Concourse of the Birds
immersePlan.text: Look at the Persian miniature of ʿAṭṭār’s poem in the Metropolitan Museum. Count the birds, and find the one that is looking at you.

immersePlan.name: Look at calligraphy of Hū
immersePlan.text: Look at a piece of calligraphy where the single word Hū, He, is shaped into an image. Notice how a letter turns into a picture. Try drawing a word you love as a shape.

immersePlan.name: Eat a few dates slowly
immersePlan.text: Eat a few dates with a glass of water, as the Prophet is said to have broken his fast. Taste the sweetness and thank the palm.

immersePlan.name: Cook mercimek çorbası
immersePlan.text: Cook red lentil soup with onion, carrot and a squeeze of lemon, as in Anatolian kitchens and lodges. Eat it with bread, and share a bowl with someone.

immersePlan.name: Make semolina halva
immersePlan.text: Toast semolina in butter, stir in warm sweetened milk, and cook until it holds together. Stir slowly, think of someone, and share it. In Turkey it is made in memory of the dead.

immersePlan.name: Make Turkish coffee
immersePlan.text: Heat finely ground coffee, water and a little sugar in a small pot until it foams, three times. Pour gently, let the grounds settle, and drink slowly. Coffee drinking began among Sufis in Yemen.

immersePlan.name: Serve çay in a small glass
immersePlan.text: Brew strong black tea and serve it in a small glass to anyone who sits down. Offer it to a guest before any question is asked. Drink yours slowly.

immersePlan.name: Stir a sharbat
immersePlan.text: Stir a rose or sour cherry cordial into cold water for a sweet drink, served to guests at shrines. Share a glass with someone, and say what you are thankful for.

immersePlan.name: Offer tea before any question
immersePlan.text: Whoever arrives today, offer tea or water before asking why they have come. If no one comes, take a cup to a neighbour. Hospitality is a practice, not an extra.

immersePlan.name: Greet with a hand on the heart
immersePlan.text: Greet someone today by placing your right hand over your heart with a slight bow. It is a greeting and a thanks. Notice how it softens the exchange.

immersePlan.name: Sit in a circle
immersePlan.text: Gather two or more people and sit in a circle, equal and facing the centre, for a few minutes of quiet or poetry. Notice how the shape changes the mood.

immersePlan.name: Play Engare
immersePlan.text: Play a few levels of the quiet puzzle game from Iran about motion and geometry. Each solution is a small pattern. If you do not have it, draw a geometric pattern with a ruler and compass.

immersePlan.name: Play backgammon
immersePlan.text: Play nard, backgammon, called tavla in Turkey and takhteh in Iran. Persian writers used the game as a picture of fate and free will. Play a short game, and accept the dice.

immersePlan.name: Play old chess
immersePlan.text: Play shatranj, old chess, where a counsellor stands where the queen now stands. Rumi used the game in his stories. Play a short game, slowly, and think of what each piece is for.

immersePlan.name: Remember the Wedding Night
immersePlan.text: Şeb-i Arus is the anniversary of Rumi’s death in December 1273, which he called his wedding night with the Beloved. Read a few of his lines about death and union, and light a candle for someone you have lost.

immersePlan.name: Listen to a sacred music festival
immersePlan.text: Look up the Fes Festival of World Sacred Music, held since 1994 in the gardens and courtyards of the old city. Play a recording from it and imagine the courtyard.

immersePlan.name: Look up the Mevlana Museum
immersePlan.text: Look up Rumi’s tomb at Konya, in the former lodge of the Mevlevi. Read a short account of what visitors do there, and notice the calm of the photographs.

immersePlan.name: Practise adab
immersePlan.text: Adab is courtesy and right conduct. Choose one place today, a shop, an office, a bus, where you will add a little more grace to every exchange than is needed. Notice what it does.

immersePlan.name: Say a word of remembrance
immersePlan.text: Dhikr is remembrance. Choose one short word or phrase and repeat it quietly whenever you wait today: at a light, in a queue, while the kettle boils. Notice how the waiting changes.

immersePlan.name: Say shukr three times
immersePlan.text: Shukr is gratitude. Say thank you, in thought or aloud, three times today for something you usually take for granted: water, a roof, a friend. Say it as if it were new.

rules.text: Begin with remembrance, end with gratitude
rules.why: The day is held between the two, as Muslims begin acts with bismillāh and close them with al-ḥamdu lillāh.
The Qur’an likens backbiting to eating the flesh of one’s dead brother. Guarding the tongue is the first discipline.

rules.text: Welcome every guest as a gift
rules.why: A saying loved by Sufis: the guest is a guest of God. Offer first, ask nothing.

rules.text: Keep one hour of the night quiet
rules.why: No screens, no talk. The heart needs dark and silence the way a seed does.

rules.text: See the fault in yourself first
rules.why: The path works on the nafs, the commanding self. Other people’s faults make a useful mirror, if you will look.
Courtesy toward everyone and everything: how you enter a room, pour water, speak of the absent.

read.why: Plain Turkish songs by an Anatolian dervish.

read.why: The classic scholarly survey, written with love.

read.title: The Garden of Truth

listen.creator: Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan
listen.why: Qawwali: devotional song of the Chishti shrines, by its greatest modern voice.

art.why: A Persian miniature of ʿAṭṭār’s poem. Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.

art.title: The Ardabil Carpet
art.creator: Made for the shrine of Shaykh Ṣafī al-Dīn
art.why: One of the oldest dated carpets in the world. Victoria and Albert Museum, London.

art.title: Calligraphy of Hū
art.creator: Ottoman calligraphers
art.why: A single word shaped into an image.

art.title: Shrine of Nizamuddin Auliya

eat.title: Dates
eat.creator: A few, with water
eat.why: The food with which the Prophet broke his fast.

eat.title: Lentil soup
eat.creator: Mercimek çorbası
eat.why: The soup of Anatolian kitchens and lodges.

eat.title: Ashure
eat.creator: Noah’s pudding
eat.why: Grains, pulses and dried fruit, cooked in a great pot and given to neighbours.

eat.title: Semolina halva
eat.creator: İrmik helvası
eat.why: Stirred slowly and shared in memory of the dead.

drink.title: Turkish coffee
drink.creator: Small, strong, unhurried
drink.why: Coffee drinking began among Sufis in Yemen, to stay awake for night devotions.

drink.title: Black tea
drink.creator: Çay, in a small glass
drink.why: Offered to anyone who sits down.

drink.title: Sharbat
drink.creator: Rose or sour cherry cordial
drink.why: A sweet drink served to guests at shrines.

customs.title: Sit in a circle
customs.creator: Equal, facing the centre
customs.why: The shape of a gathering for remembrance.

customs.title: Remove shoes at the door
customs.creator: Keep the space clean
customs.why: As in any mosque, lodge or home.

customs.title: Hand on the heart
customs.creator: A greeting and a thanks
customs.why: The right hand placed over the heart with a slight bow.

customs.title: Feed whoever comes
customs.creator: The shrine kitchen
customs.why: South Asian shrines serve free food daily to all, without asking who they are.

customs.title: Visit as a guest
customs.creator: At a shrine or public gathering
customs.why: Dress modestly, follow the lead of those present, and ask before photographing.

games.title: Engare
games.creator: Video game · Mahdi Bahrami
games.why: A quiet puzzle game from Iran about motion and geometry. Each solution draws a piece of the patterns found on mosque tiles.

games.title: Nard
games.creator: Board game · Persia
games.why: Backgammon, called tavla in Turkey and takhteh in Iran. Persian writers read the board as fate and the moves as choice.

games.title: Shatranj
games.creator: Board game · Persia and the Islamic world
games.why: Old chess, with a counsellor where the queen now stands. Rumi used its moves as images for the soul’s defeats that turn out to be wins.

festivals.title: Şeb-i Arus
festivals.creator: 7 to 17 December, Konya, Turkey
festivals.why: The wedding night: the anniversary of Rumi’s death in 1273, which he called a reunion. The whirling ceremony is performed each evening.

festivals.title: Urs of Moinuddin Chishti
festivals.creator: First six days of Rajab, Ajmer, India
festivals.why: The death anniversary of the saint of Ajmer. Pilgrims of every faith bring flowers and cloth, and devotional music runs through the night.

festivals.title: Mawlid
festivals.creator: 12 Rabi al-awwal
festivals.why: The Prophet’s birthday, kept in many Sufi communities with poetry, lights and shared food.

festivals.title: Fes Festival of World Sacred Music
festivals.creator: Early summer, Fes, Morocco
festivals.why: Since 1994, concerts in the gardens and courtyards of the old city, with Sufi nights after dark.

places.title: Mevlana Museum
places.creator: Konya, Turkey
places.why: Rumi’s tomb under a turquoise dome, in the former lodge of the Mevlevi order. Visitors and pilgrims stand side by side.

places.title: Nizamuddin Dargah
places.creator: Delhi, India
places.why: The shrine of Nizamuddin Auliya, with the poet Amir Khusrau buried nearby. Devotional singing fills the courtyard on Thursday evenings.

places.title: Ajmer Sharif Dargah
places.creator: Ajmer, Rajasthan, India
places.why: The tomb of Moinuddin Chishti, one of the most visited shrines in South Asia.

places.title: Galata Mevlevi Lodge
places.creator: Istanbul, Turkey
places.why: A dervish lodge from 1491, now a museum with an octagonal ceremonial hall where the whirling ceremony is shown.

places.title: Mausoleum of Khoja Ahmed Yasawi
places.creator: Turkistan, Kazakhstan
places.why: The vast unfinished tomb Timur ordered for the twelfth-century poet and teacher of the Turkic world. A World Heritage Site.

ethics.title: Love as the path
ethics.text: Rābiʿa asked to love God for God’s own sake, with no eye on reward or punishment. For the Sufis love is both the road and the arrival.
ethics.practice: Do one good thing today with no thought of what comes back.

ethics.title: Serve first
ethics.text: Before any teaching, the novice sweeps, cooks and carries. Service wears down the self that wants to be special.
ethics.practice: Take the lowest task in the room today, and do it well.

ethics.title: Humility before the guide
ethics.text: The path is not walked alone or by cleverness. One learns from those who have gone ahead, and from everyone.
ethics.practice: Ask someone for correction today, and take it.

ethics.title: Generosity
ethics.text: What passes through your hands was never yours. A dervish is known by an open hand.

ethics.title: Guard the tongue
ethics.text: No gossip, no boasting, no needless complaint. Speak only what is true and kind, or keep silence.
ethics.practice: Notice the first thing you want to say about someone absent, and do not say it.

ethics.title: The children of Adam are one body
ethics.text: Saʿdī: if one limb is hurt, the others cannot rest. One who is unmoved by another’s pain does not deserve the name human.
ethics.practice: Let one piece of bad news about strangers actually reach you today.

philosophy.title: Unity of being
philosophy.text: There is one reality, and the many things are its self-disclosures. This teaching is associated with Ibn ʿArabī, though the phrase came from his followers.
philosophy.practice: Look at three unlike things today as faces of one.

philosophy.title: The heart as mirror
philosophy.text: The heart was made to reflect the Real. Heedlessness and self-regard rust it. Remembrance is the polish.
philosophy.practice: What clouded your heart today? What cleared it?

philosophy.title: Dying before you die
philosophy.text: A saying dear to Sufis: die before you die. Let the grasping self go now, by choice, and what remains is free.
philosophy.practice: Give up being right in one argument.

philosophy.title: Longing as teacher
philosophy.text: The reed cries because it was cut from the reed bed. Longing is not a problem to be solved. It is the pull of home.
philosophy.practice: Sit with a longing for five minutes without trying to satisfy it.

philosophy.title: The stations of the path
philosophy.text: Repentance, patience, gratitude, trust, contentment, love: stations reached by effort, lit by states that come as gifts.
philosophy.practice: Which station are you working at now?

philosophy.title: The self that commands
philosophy.text: The nafs begins by ordering you about, learns to blame itself, and can come to rest. The path is its education.
philosophy.practice: Catch the commanding self once today, and name it.

philosophy.title: Outward and inward
philosophy.text: Every act has a form and a meaning. The Sufis kept the form and went looking for the meaning.
philosophy.practice: Do one habitual act today with full awareness of why.

philosophy.title: Wherever you turn
philosophy.text: The Qur’an says: wherever you turn, there is the face of God. Nothing is outside the sacred.
philosophy.practice: Find it in the least likely place you go today.

philosophy.title: The guest house
philosophy.text: Rumi compares a human being to an inn where joys and sorrows arrive as guests. Welcome them all. Each has been sent.
philosophy.practice: Greet today’s unwelcome feeling as a guest.

philosophy.title: Trust
philosophy.text: Do your work fully and leave the result. The Prophet’s saying: tie your camel, then trust in God.
philosophy.practice: What are you gripping that is not yours to control?

intro: Sufism, taṣawwuf in Arabic, is the inner, contemplative dimension of Islam. Where the law asks what a Muslim should do, the Sufi asks how to do it with a present heart, and how to come to know the One being worshipped.

It began in the first Islamic centuries among ascetics in Iraq and Syria who answered the wealth of the new empire with poverty, night vigils and constant remembrance of God. The name probably comes from ṣūf, the coarse wool they wore. Within a few generations a note of love entered and changed everything. Rābiʿa of Basra, a freed slave, prayed to love God not from fear of hell or hope of paradise but for God’s own sake.

By the tenth and eleventh centuries the Sufis had a vocabulary and a map. The seeker travels through stations, repentance, patience, gratitude, trust, love, and is visited by states that come as grace. The obstacle is the nafs, the self-centred self. The organ of knowing is the heart. The goal is fanāʾ, the passing away of the self’s claims in awareness of God, and baqāʾ, abiding in God while living in the world. The great theologian al-Ghazālī, after a crisis that left him unable to teach, found certainty among the Sufis and wrote their practice into the mainstream of Islamic thought.

From the twelfth century the path was organised into orders, each tracing a chain of teachers back to the Prophet Muhammad: the Qādiriyya, the Chishtiyya in India with its devotional music, the Naqshbandiyya with its silent remembrance, the Mevleviyya of Anatolia with its turning ceremony. The orders built lodges, fed the poor, and carried Islam across Africa, Central Asia and the Indian Ocean. Their teaching was often given in verse, which is why Sufism gave the world some of its greatest poets: ʿAṭṭār, Rumi, Saʿdī, Hafez, Yunus Emre.

Rumi is the best known. A scholar in thirteenth-century Konya, he was overturned in 1244 by meeting a wandering dervish, Shams of Tabriz, and poured the experience into the Masnavi, some twenty-five thousand couplets of stories and teaching. Many popular English "Rumi" quotations are loose versions made by writers who did not read Persian, and they tend to leave out the Islam. Read him in a scholarly translation at least once.

This Onda borrows four things any respectful guest may do: sit in remembrance, read the poets aloud, listen, and keep the night quiet. Sufism is a living tradition of practising Muslims, taught by authorised guides and under pressure in many countries. Its rituals belong to its orders. If the path calls you, go and meet them.
guide.origin: The Islamic world, from Arabia and Iraq to Persia, Anatolia, India and Africa

figures.name: Rābiʿa al-ʿAdawiyya
figures.bio: Saint of Basra who made selfless love of God the centre of the path.

figures.name: al-Junayd
figures.bio: Master of the "sober" school in Baghdad. Most later orders trace themselves through him.

figures.name: al-Ḥallāj
figures.bio: Ecstatic executed in Baghdad after saying "I am the Truth".

figures.name: al-Ghazālī
figures.bio: Jurist and theologian whose Revival of the Religious Sciences reconciled Sufism and law.

figures.name: ʿAbd al-Qādir al-Jīlānī
figures.bio: Preacher of Baghdad and namesake of the Qādirī order, the most widespread of all.

figures.name: Farīd al-Dīn ʿAṭṭār
figures.bio: Apothecary-poet of Nishapur. Author of The Conference of the Birds.

figures.name: Ibn ʿArabī
figures.bio: Andalusian known as "the Greatest Master". Wrote hundreds of works on the unity of being.

figures.name: Muʿīn al-Dīn Chishtī
figures.bio: Brought the Chishti order to India. His shrine at Ajmer draws pilgrims of every religion.

figures.name: Jalāl al-Dīn Rūmī
figures.bio: Persian poet and teacher of Konya, called Mevlana, "our master".

figures.name: Shams-i Tabrīzī
figures.bio: The wandering dervish whose friendship transformed Rumi.

figures.name: Yunus Emre
figures.bio: Anatolian dervish whose songs founded Turkish literature.

figures.name: Ḥāfeẓ
figures.bio: Lyric poet of Shiraz whose collected poems are consulted like an oracle in Iranian homes.

history.what: The ascetics of Basra and Kufa
history.detail: Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and others preach renunciation and fear of God. Rābiʿa turns the emphasis to love.
His cry "I am the Truth" was read as blasphemy by the authorities and as the voice of one emptied of self by later Sufis.
A handbook defining the Sufis’ terms and arguing that the path is rooted in the Qur’an and the Prophet’s example.

history.what: al-Ghazālī leaves his chair and writes the Revival
history.detail: After a breakdown he spends a decade in retreat and travel. His forty-book work makes inward religion part of Sunni orthodoxy.
Followers of ʿAbd al-Qādir al-Jīlānī and other masters organise into brotherhoods with lodges, initiations and chains of transmission.

history.what: ʿAṭṭār completes The Conference of the Birds
history.detail: Thirty birds survive the journey to find the Simorgh, whose name in Persian means "thirty birds".
Muʿīn al-Dīn Chishtī settles at Ajmer. The order welcomes all comers and uses music in devotion: the origin of qawwali.

history.what: Ibn ʿArabī writes The Bezels of Wisdom
history.detail: In Damascus, late in a life that began in Murcia. The book becomes the most commented-upon text of Sufi metaphysics.
Three years later Shams disappears. Rumi’s grief becomes the Dīvān of Shams, and later the Masnavi, begun around 1258.
The night is remembered as his "wedding night", the reunion with the Beloved. His son Sultan Walad organises the Mevlevi order.
Bahāʾ al-Dīn Naqshband of Bukhara teaches silent remembrance and "solitude in the crowd". His order spreads from Turkey to China.
Sufis in Yemen adopt coffee to stay alert through night devotions. From their lodges it spreads to Mecca, Cairo and Istanbul.
The new republic bans the Sufi orders. The Mevlevi ceremony returns in the 1950s as a public commemoration held in Konya each December.

history.what: The Mevlevi sema is inscribed by UNESCO
history.detail: Listed as intangible cultural heritage of humanity. The year 2007, eight centuries after Rumi’s birth, had been named for him.

concepts.detail: The Qur’an commands it repeatedly. The orders differ in method: aloud or silent, alone or in a circle, with or without movement and music. All agree that the tongue’s remembrance is meant to become the heart’s.
The classical image is a circle. The law is the rim, the path is the radius, and reality is the centre. You cannot reach the centre without standing on the rim.
Not the annihilation of the person, but of the illusion that one exists apart from God. The mature Sufi returns to ordinary life, transformed.
The Qur’an names a self that commands to evil, a self that blames itself and a self at peace. The Sufis made these a map of inner work.
Not the emotions. A subtle organ that can be veiled or unveiled. A saying holds that heaven and earth cannot contain God, but the heart of the believer can.

concepts.text: The motive of creation and the way back.
concepts.detail: A tradition much quoted by Sufis has God say: I was a hidden treasure and I loved to be known, so I created the world.
The doctrine of Ibn ʿArabī’s school. Critics feared it erased the difference between Creator and creation. Its defenders say it means that nothing has being of its own.

concepts.text: Knowledge passes from heart to heart.
concepts.detail: Each order keeps a silsila, a chain of names from the present shaykh back to the Prophet. Allegiance to a guide is the formal start of the path.
Contested among Muslims and among Sufis. The Chishtis and Mevlevis embraced it under strict conditions of time, place and company; the Naqshbandis mostly avoided it.
Right behaviour toward God, the teacher, companions, guests and oneself. Often called the whole of the path.

facts.text: In Turkey, Iran and Afghanistan, Rumi is not called Rumi. He is Mevlana or Mawlānā, "our master", or Balkhī, after his family’s home. "Rumi" means "from Rome", that is, from Anatolia.
The famous lines beginning "Come, come, whoever you are" are not found in the earliest manuscripts of Rumi. They are usually credited to an earlier Persian Sufi, Abū Saʿīd Abū al-Khayr.
In the Mevlevi ceremony the tall felt hat stands for the tombstone of the ego, the white skirt for its shroud, and the black cloak that is dropped for the grave.
The whirling dervish holds the right palm up to receive and the left palm down to give.
Many "Rumi" and "Hafez" quotations online have no source in the Persian. Some popular English Hafez books are original poems by a modern American author.
The word coffee comes through Turkish from Arabic qahwa. Its first recorded drinkers were Yemeni Sufis.
A carpet bearing Saʿdī’s lines on the children of Adam was presented to the United Nations in New York by Iran.

glossary.meaning: The order founded by Rumi’s followers, known for the turning ceremony.
Devotional music of the South Asian Sufi shrines.
The shrine built over a saint’s tomb, especially in South Asia.
The chain of teachers linking a shaykh to the Prophet.
A long poem in rhyming couplets. Rumi’s is the Masnavi.
The mythical bird that is the goal of ʿAṭṭār’s birds.

sensitivity.note: Sufism is the contemplative heart of Islam and a living tradition of practising Muslims. This Onda offers remembrance, poetry, listening and night stillness in a form open to anyone, and does not reproduce the rituals of any order.
requiredCaveats: The dhikr circles, initiations and the Mevlevi turning ceremony belong to the orders and are learned from an authorised guide. Do not imitate them.
Many popular English "Rumi" and "Hafez" quotations are loose versions or inventions. Prefer translations made from Persian.
If you are not Muslim, practice as a respectful guest. If you are, follow your own tradition’s guidance.
